predecessors.name: Yuan dynasty
predecessors.text: Central Tibet, ruled under the Yuan by the Sakya lamas until the Phagmodrupa 'superseded Sakya in the period 1354-1358'

successors.name: People's Republic of China
successors.text: Tibet as the Seventeen Point Agreement of 23 May 1951 left it: Ue-Tsang under the Tibetan government, and Chamdo and western Kham, taken by the PLA in October 1950 and 'placed under the authority of…

ledger.x: 1354: Changchub Gyaltsen's Phagmodrupa regime takes central Tibet from the Sakya and rules from Nedong.
1358: Sakya rule over Tibet ends.
1435: the Rinpungpa ministers of Tsang take the power from the Phagmodrupa princes; the state and its land continue.
1565: the Tsangpa of Shigatse overthrow the Rinpungpa and rule Tibet.
1565: the seat moves to Shigatse (Samdruptse).
1612-13: the Tsangpa ruler Karma Phuntsok Namgyal subdues western Tsang and West Tibet.
ledger.cp: Latö Lho and Latö Chang (western Tsang) and the other West Tibetan regimes

ledger.x: 1619: the Tsangpa conquer Mangyül Gungthang.
1641: Güshi Khan's war on the Tsangpa begins.
1642: Kham comes under the Dalai Lama's government with the grant of temporal power.
1642: the Ganden Phodrang government of the 5th Dalai Lama replaces the Tsangpa; Tibet is a Khoshut protectorate.
1642: Lhasa becomes the capital.
March 1642: Shigatse falls and the Tsangpa end.
1679: Tibet goes to war with Ladakh.
1681: Tawang enters Tibet's orbit.
1684: the Treaty of Tingmosgang ends the war.
1684: Guge is annexed to Tibet.
August 1717: the Dzungars enter Tibet.
December 1717: the fighting ends with the fall of the Potala.
December 1717: the Dzungars hold Tibet under a military government.
1720: the Qing drive the Dzungars out and Qing protection begins.
1727: Kham east of the Dri River goes to Sichuan.
1788: Gorkha troops invade Tibet.
1789: the Treaty of Kerung.
1791: the second Gorkha invasion.
2 October 1792: the Treaty of Betrawati.
December 1903: the British expedition crosses into Tibet.
7 September 1904: the Convention of Lhasa.
September 1904: Britain holds the Chumbi Valley.
1905: China sets out to 'reintegrate' Kham.
8 February 1908: Britain leaves the Chumbi Valley.
1910: the Qing occupy Lhasa.
August 1912: Qing forces leave central Tibet.
1912: the Qing fall, and Chinese control of western Kham passes to the Republic.
1912: Chamdo and western Kham stay in Chinese hands under the Republic until 1918.
1913: the 13th Dalai Lama proclaims Tibet independent.
3 July 1914: the Simla Convention cedes Tawang on paper.
1918: the Chinese occupation of western Kham ends and Lhasa holds the land again.
May-June 1930: the Sino-Tibetan War opens.
1933: the truces.
1944: British India extends its administration into the Tawang tract.
1947: the Raj ends (Cliopatria's British Raj row ends in 1947).
1947: the Raj ends (Cliopatria's British Raj row ends in 1947).
October 1950: the PLA takes Chamdo.
23 May 1951: Chamdo passes into the PRC.
23 May 1951: the Seventeen Point Agreement ends Tibet's independence.

wars.name: Gushi Khan's conquest of Tibet
wars.outcome: Gushi Khan destroys the Beri king in Kham (winter 1640-41) and the Tsangpa at Shigatse (March 1642); the 5th Dalai Lama is given the temporal power and Tibet becomes a Khoshut protectorate.

wars.name: Tibet-Ladakh-Mughal War
wars.outcome: Treaty of Tingmosgang (1684): the border is fixed at the Lhari stream near Demchok and Guge goes to Tibet; Ladakh reduced to its present borders.

wars.name: Dzungar conquest of Tibet
wars.outcome: Lha-bzang Khan killed 2 December 1717; Dzungar military government until the Qing expedition under Yunti expelled them in 1720.

wars.name: Sino-Nepalese War
wars.outcome: Gorkha invasions of 1788 and 1791 end in the Treaty of Kerung (1789) and the Treaty of Betrawati (2 October 1792); status quo ante bellum, Nepal a Qing tributary.

wars.name: Sino-Sikh War (Dogra invasion of Tibet)
wars.outcome: The Dogras 'attempted to establish their authority on U-Tsang but were defeated in the Sino-Sikh War (1841-1842)'.

wars.name: British expedition to Tibet
wars.outcome: Convention of Lhasa (7 September 1904): indemnity, recognition of the Sikkim-Tibet border, the Chumbi Valley held until the indemnity was paid (8 February 1908).

wars.name: Zhao Erfeng's Kham campaign and the Qing occupation of Lhasa
wars.outcome: Kham 'reintegrated' into China from 1905 (or 1908); Lhasa occupied and the 13th Dalai Lama deposed in 1910; Qing forces surrender in the summer of 1912 (Three Point Agreement, 12 August 1912).

wars.name: Simla Convention and the McMahon Line dispute over Tawang
wars.outcome: No fighting: the 1914 Simla Accord defined the McMahon Line and Tibet 'relinquished several hundred square miles of its territory, including Tawang' on paper, but China did not recognise the treaty; the British sent a small column in 1938 and extended…

wars.name: Tibetan recovery of Chamdo and western Kham
wars.outcome: 'Lhasa regained control of Chamdo and western Kham.

wars.name: Sino-Tibetan War
wars.outcome: Chinese victory: the Tibetans are pushed back across the Jinsha and the Upper Yangtze becomes the border; truces of 1933.

wars.name: Battle of Chamdo and the annexation of Tibet
wars.outcome: The PLA crosses the Jinsha on 6-7 October 1950 and takes Chamdo by 19 October; the Seventeen Point Agreement of 23 May 1951 affirms Chinese sovereignty.

certainty.note: The frontier of Ü-Tsang is approximate throughout (Kham is outside the state until 1642, Amdo, Kokonor and the Qaidam Basin always, Guge until 1684, Latö until 1612 and Mangyül Gungthang until 1619; the Ming and Tibetan lines are not dated…
The western border is sharp from the 1684 Treaty of Tingmosgang ('the Lhari stream near Demchok'); the eastern and northern frontiers are soft.
